mcqs.question: What problem does Unicode solve that ASCII and code pages couldn't?
options: Unicode makes text files smaller than ASCII
Unicode assigns a single, unambiguous code point to every character across every script, instead of different code pages reusing the same byte values for different characters
Unicode removes the need for any encoding when storing text as bytes
Unicode only works for European languages, same as ASCII
mcqs.explanation: The core problem with code pages was ambiguity -- the same byte value meant a different character depending on which code page was assumed. Unicode fixes this by giving every character one unambiguous code point; how those code points become bytes is still a separate encoding question (UTF-8, etc).

mcqs.question: In UTF-8, how can you tell that a byte is a continuation byte rather than the start of a character?
options: A continuation byte's top two bits are always 10, distinguishing it from every leading-byte pattern
Continuation bytes only appear at the end of a string
There's no way to tell without decoding from the start of the string
mcqs.explanation: UTF-8 reserves the bit pattern 10xxxxxx exclusively for continuation bytes -- no leading byte ever starts with those two bits, which is exactly what lets you find a character boundary starting from any byte position.

mcqs.question: Why is truncating a UTF-8 string at a fixed byte offset risky?
options: UTF-8 strings cannot be truncated at all
The cut point can fall in the middle of a multi-byte character, producing invalid or corrupted text
Byte-offset truncation only works for UTF-16, not UTF-8
It always deletes the first character of the string instead of the last
mcqs.explanation: Since UTF-8 characters can span 1 to 4 bytes, cutting at an arbitrary byte offset can slice through a multi-byte sequence, leaving a broken partial character (and sometimes invalid UTF-8) at the boundary.
